## Ecological Background

The European gypsy moth (*Lymantria dispar*) is a defoliator native to Europe where it causes substantial disturbance especially on oaks (McManus & Csóka, 2007). Introduced to North America in 1869, it became an invasive pest in northeastern oak forests (Elkinton & Liebhold, 1990).

While adult females are poor dispersers, first-instar larvae balloon passively over short distances via wind (Hunter & Elkinton, 2000), complemented by human-aided long-distance transport in invaded ranges (Liebhold et al., 1992). Each larva consumes roughly 3–4 g of foliage during single-season development (Sharov & Colbert, 1996), with outbreaks typically lasting several years at 8–12 year intervals (Johnson et al., 2005).

## Model Implementation

Dispersal is approximated with a Gaussian kernel (`maxDistance: 50` m) parameterized from Elderd et al. (2013), and cell colonization requires at least 500 growing degree days (`GDD10 > 500`) alongside Common oak (`quro`).

Periodic outbreak cyclicity is driven directly via `BiteLifeCycle` (`outbreakStart: 'rnd(8,12)'`, `outbreakDuration: 'rnd(2,4)'`). In `BiteBiomass`, both `growthRateFunction` and antagonist-induced `mortality` respond sigmoidally to `outbreakYears` (Lustig et al., 2017). Foliage consumption acts on both saplings and trees, removing foliage from shortest trees upward until annual demand (`agentImpact`) is met.
